facts.claim: "Foolish and Blue" was written by Keshia Bailey and Allen Thompson.
The Bandcamp credits list Allen Thompson and Gordon Persha as producers, Persha as mixer, and Chris Frasco as mastering engineer at Master Frasco Audio Lab.
The Bandcamp credits say it was recorded at Thunder Sound Studios in Franklin, Kentucky.

Credited players: Thompson, Bailey, Dana Kalan and Olivia Burnett on vocals; Paul Thacker and Rob Crowell on sax; Diego Vasquez on trombone; Robert Gay on trumpet; Jimmy Matt Rowland on keys; Gordon Persha on bass; Clint Maine and Mike Ford Jr. on guitars; Ray Dunham on drums.
The single was released June 19, 2020 on Cafe Rooster Records, runs about 4:44, and Apple Music classes it as roots rock.
Thompson said it was the first song he and Bailey wrote together. Bailey came up with the title, and the two finished the song in about 20 minutes.
Bailey said she was a little heartbroken when she and Thompson wrote the song. She also described writing it with her best friend, and said singing through the heartache helped her.

It was the band's first single on Cafe Rooster Records and was released digitally only. A Norwegian blog says the planned vinyl was dropped because of the COVID crisis in the US. It was paired with the single "Heartache".
The song was later included on the band's debut album The Future Looks Fine (September 2021).

LadyCouch is a Nashville band co-founded by Keshia Bailey (formerly of Magnolia Sons) and Allen Thompson (of the Allen Thompson Band). Thompson says it grew out of his previous band, which he ended at The Basement East in August 2018.

draft:
Two voices lean on the same note in **Foolish and Blue**, and that pairing makes the song's case before anything else does. A slightly raspy, mid-range lead holds its lines long and steady. A higher voice settles in beside it, sometimes in unison, sometimes a close step above. It sounds like company. That fits how the song came to be. Keshia Bailey has said she was a little heartbroken when she wrote it with Allen Thompson, whom she described as her best friend, and that singing through the heartache helped.

The title was Bailey's idea, and it holds two feelings that never cancel out. "Blue" is the hurt. "Foolish" is the part that stings worse, the embarrassment of having let yourself get there in the first place. A song named for that pairing isn't asking for pity so much as owning up, and the harmony keeps the owning-up from sounding lonely. Thompson says it was the first song the two wrote together and that they finished it in about 20 minutes. Nothing here sounds labored over.

The band plays it slow, with a sway rather than a march. A clean electric guitar rolls through arpeggiated chords. The bass walks underneath instead of parking on the root, which keeps the sadness moving. The drums stay soft, a snare marking time and a ride cymbal adding a little shimmer. The room is medium-sized and warm, with enough reverb to put air around everything and enough separation that you can follow each part. It's polished, maybe smoother than some listeners want their heartbreak, but the gloss reads as care, not distance.

LadyCouch is a big Nashville outfit, built on the model of The Band, Little Feat and the Grateful Dead. The credits for this one read like a roll call. Thompson, Bailey, Dana Kalan and Olivia Burnett are on vocals, with two saxes, trombone and trumpet. Jimmy Matt Rowland plays keys, Clint Maine and Mike Ford Jr. play guitar and Ray Dunham plays drums. Gordon Persha plays bass and co-produced with Thompson, then mixed it. They cut it at Thunder Sound Studios in Franklin, Kentucky. Bailey brought East Tennessee mountain music, gospel, soul and delta blues into the group, and the gospel side shows in how the voices work together. The second voice answers the first the way a congregation answers a preacher.

The song later found a home on the band's debut album, *The Future Looks Fine*, a fitting title for a record that holds a song about getting through it.

It sticks because it lets you admit you were a fool without having to admit it alone.
